Wisconsin Squatters Rights and Adverse Possession: What Owners Should Know

Can a squatter take ownership of a Wisconsin house?

Yes, but only after meeting every element of a Wisconsin adverse possession statute for a long, uninterrupted stretch. The law sets periods of 20, 10 or 7 years depending on the facts, and the occupant has to prove they fit within one of them.

The title holder starts with the advantage. Under sec. 893.30, a person with legal title is presumed to have been in possession within the time the law requires. Anyone else's occupation is treated as subordinate to that title unless they held the land adversely for 7, 10 or 20 years before a lawsuit. If someone moves into your Wisconsin house without consent, a few months of staying put gains them nothing.

Tenants are a special case. Under sec. 893.31, a tenant's possession counts as the landlord's possession until 10 years after the tenancy ends, or 10 years after the last rent payment when there was no written lease. The adverse possession clocks do not start until that period is over.

Time periods for adverse possession

The basic period is 20 years. It drops to 10 years when the claimant holds a recorded written instrument, and to 7 years when that claim is paired with payment of every real estate tax.

StatutePeriodMain requirements
Sec. 893.2520 yearsActual continued occupation under claim of title, exclusive of any other right, covering only the part actually occupied that is enclosed by a substantial enclosure or usually cultivated or improved
Sec. 893.2610 yearsEntry in good faith under a written instrument or court judgment, recorded with the register of deeds within 30 days of entry, with continued occupation of a material portion of the land described
Sec. 893.277 yearsThe 10-year requirements, plus recording within 30 days of execution and payment of all real estate taxes for the 7 years after original entry

Claimants can add their time to that of earlier occupants they succeeded, so a claim may rest on more than one person's years. A successful claimant can bring an action under ch. 841 to establish title. Under the 20-year rule a claim reaches only land actually occupied. Under the 10-year rule it reaches the land described in the instrument, except that possession of one lot in a divided tract is not possession of another lot.

What counts as possession

Possession means actual, continued occupation under a claim of title. For the written-instrument rules in secs. 893.26 and 893.27, Wisconsin lists facts that show possession, and the list is not exhaustive.

  • The land has been usually cultivated or improved.
  • The land has been protected by a substantial enclosure.
  • Although not enclosed, the land has been used for fuel or fencing timber, or for the ordinary use of the occupant.
  • Where a known farm or single lot is partly improved, the part not cleared or enclosed is treated as occupied for the same time as the improved part, following the usual course and custom of the adjoining country.

Good faith is presumed at entry under the written instrument rules unless someone rebuts it. The 20-year rule has no good faith requirement. A person who enters under a deed they know is fraudulent can still start the 20-year period, but not the 10-year one.

Court decisions attached to the statute add that acts consistent with sporadic trespass do not tell an owner that someone is claiming the land. The test is whether the use gave a reasonably diligent owner notice of an ownership claim.

How can a Wisconsin owner stop an adverse possession claim?

An owner can interrupt the clock by recording an affidavit of interruption, by starting a court action, or by ending the possession in time. Act well before the 20, 10 or 7 years run out.

Sec. 893.305 sets out the affidavit route. The record title holder records an affidavit along with a survey certified no more than 5 years before recording, gives the notice the statute requires, and records proof of that notice. The affidavit gives a legal description, states that the owner is the record title holder, describes the possession being interrupted and says a new period may begin the day after recording. Notice goes by certified mail to a known occupant or neighbor, and by published notice if the person is unknown. When the occupant is a neighbor, the owner must also record a notice of the affidavit against the neighbor's abutting parcel within 90 days after the neighbor receives notice. Recording the affidavit is not an admission that the possession is adverse.

Sec. 893.32 covers entry on the land. A simple entry interrupts a claim only if the owner starts an action against the possessor within one year after the entry and before the limitation period runs, or if the entry actually ends the possession and the owner takes possession. The affidavit procedure is not the only way to interrupt a claim.

Public land is off limits. Under sec. 893.29, no title to land belonging to the state or to a city, village, town, county or school district can be gained by adverse possession.

What to do about a trespasser or someone living in your property

Tell the occupant to leave in clear terms, put the notice in writing, and call local law enforcement if the person stays. Wisconsin defines trespass to land in sec. 943.13, and a violation is a Class B forfeiture.

A person commits trespass by entering enclosed, cultivated or undeveloped land of another without the express or implied consent of the owner or occupant. Entering or remaining after being told by the owner or occupant not to do so is also trespass. The notice can be given personally, orally or in writing, or by posting. Posting means a sign at least 11 inches square in at least 2 conspicuous places for every 40 acres, naming the owner or occupant, or markings that read private land together with the owner's name.

If the occupant was ever a tenant, the circuit court clerk can explain the eviction process. When someone leaves belongings behind in residential rental property, sec. 704.055 requires the landlord to hold them for 7 days from the date they are discovered. After that the landlord may dispose of them, but must return them promptly if the former occupant asks before disposal. The occupant, another owner or a secured party can redeem the property before disposal by paying the landlord's expenses.

Talk to a Wisconsin attorney before you change locks or remove anyone's belongings. If the person refuses to leave, the clerk's office or a lawyer can walk you through the court process.

Selling with a squatter or title dispute

An occupant or a claim to part of the land can slow a sale. Sort out who has the right to be in the house first, and gather your records of ownership, tax payments and any notices you sent.

An owner with an occupant who has no right to be there, a boundary dispute or an unrecorded claim can still sell to a cash home buyer as-is once the title company has reviewed the situation. Ask the buyer's title company what it needs before a closing date is set.

A practical order of work looks like this:

  • Pull your deed and tax payment records and confirm they match the parcel you are selling.
  • Write down when you last visited the property and who has been there since.
  • Send written notice to any occupant and keep a copy.
  • Give the title company the full story so nothing surfaces late in the closing.

If the house is vacant, secure it, keep the taxes current and record any deeds right away. Under sec. 706.08 an unrecorded conveyance is void against a later good faith purchaser for value whose conveyance is recorded first.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Wisconsin houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

How many years of occupation does adverse possession need in Wisconsin?

Twenty years under sec. 893.25 in the basic case. It is 10 years if the claimant entered in good faith under a written instrument or judgment recorded within 30 days, and 7 years if the claimant also paid all real estate taxes for the 7 years after entry.

Do squatters have rights to a Wisconsin house after a few months?

No. The shortest adverse possession period in Wisconsin is 7 years, and it requires a recorded instrument and payment of all taxes. A person who stays without consent can be a trespasser under sec. 943.13.

Can someone claim land owned by a city or county in Wisconsin?

No. Sec. 893.29 bars adverse possession of land belonging to the state or to a city, village, town, county or school district.

What should I do with belongings a trespasser leaves behind?

A landlord of residential rental property must hold them for 7 days from the date they are discovered under sec. 704.055. After that the landlord may dispose of them, but must return them promptly if the owner asks before disposal.

Can a tenant claim my Wisconsin property by adverse possession?

A tenant's possession is treated as the landlord's. Under sec. 893.31, the adverse possession periods do not start until 10 years after the tenancy ends, or 10 years after the last rent payment if there was no written lease.

Selling a Wisconsin House? Get a Cash Offer

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Laws that cover Wisconsin rentals

Two sets of rules carry most of the load: chapter 704 of the Wisconsin Statutes and chapter ATCP 134 of the Administrative Code. Chapter 704 deals with repairs, ending a tenancy, security deposits and what a transfer does to a lease. Chapter ATCP 134, run by the Department of Agriculture, Trade and Consumer Protection, governs residential rental practices.

ATCP 134 covers dwelling units statewide, with a short list of exclusions: institutional units, units occupied under a contract of sale, tourist or transient stays under 60 days, and government-owned and operated units. A tenant who loses money because of a violation can sue directly and recover twice the loss plus costs and attorney fees.

For someone selling a rental, these rules settle what the buyer takes on, how much time a tenant must get, and what has to be returned from a deposit.

What a sale does to the lease

The lease normally survives. Wis. Stat. 704.09 allows a landlord's interest to be transferred unless the lease expressly limits that power, and a limit is read as covering voluntary transfers only unless it also names transfers by operation of law.

  • Lease covenants that are not personal to the original parties can be enforced by or against the successor.
  • A successor answers in damages only for breaches during the successor's own ownership, unless the successor agrees to more by contract.
  • The seller remains responsible for lease obligations unless the lease or an express release says otherwise.
  • Remedies that existed between the original landlord and tenant carry over to or against a successor.

So a cash buyer who takes a rented house steps into the lease. Hand over a copy of each lease and a ledger of rent and deposits.

Notice before a tenancy ends

The length of notice depends on the tenancy type and the reason. The shortest common one is 5 days for unpaid rent, while a periodic tenancy needs 28 days in writing to end without cause.

SituationNotice required
Month-to-month or week-to-week, unpaid rentPay or vacate on a date at least 5 days after notice
Month-to-month tenant in default on rentVacate notice at least 14 days after giving
Lease of one year or less, unpaid rentPay or vacate at least 5 days after notice; 14 days if repeated within one year
Lease of one year or less, other breachRemedy or vacate at least 5 days after notice
Lease of more than one yearAt least 30 days to pay, repair or comply
Criminal activity threatening othersVacate at least 5 days after notice, no chance to remedy
Periodic tenancy, no causeAt least 28 days in writing, ending at the end of a rental period

Time counts from the day notice is given, and mail within the state is treated as given on the 2nd day after mailing. For a breach other than rent, a tenant complies by promptly taking reasonable steps to fix the problem.

How an eviction works after the notice runs out

The landlord files an eviction action in court. A judgment is followed by a writ of restitution, which the sheriff carries out. Under Wis. Stat. 799.40, the person entitled to possession, or an agent authorized in writing, can start the case.

  • Post office proof of certified mailing is enough to show a termination notice was properly given, and no affidavit of service can be demanded.
  • A landlord who takes past due rent after serving notice or filing does not lose the action on that ground.
  • If the court finds the plaintiff entitled to possession, it enters judgment and orders a writ of restitution to issue right away.
  • A writ cannot be carried out if the sheriff receives it more than 30 days after issue.
  • Where hardship is shown, the court can stay the writ for up to 30 days, conditioned on the tenant paying unpaid rent and the reasonable value of occupancy.

Under s. 799.45(1) the sheriff may require a deposit toward removal costs, unless the landlord says the landlord will remove and store or dispose of the property.

Belongings left behind

Wis. Stat. 704.05(5) lets a landlord presume that property left by a departed or evicted tenant is abandoned and dispose of it as the landlord chooses, unless the written agreement says otherwise.

  • Prescription medication and prescription medical equipment must be held for 7 days, and returned promptly if the tenant asks before disposal.
  • A manufactured home, mobile home or titled vehicle calls for written notice of intent to dispose to the tenant and to any secured party the landlord knows about.
  • A landlord not planning to store belongings must say so in writing when the tenant signs or renews a lease.
  • The tenant or a secured party can get the property back before disposal by paying the landlord's expenses.

Repairs and landlord entry

A landlord has to keep the parts of the premises under the landlord's control in reasonable repair and make needed structural repairs. For residential tenancies the landlord must also meet the local housing code. These duties come from s. 704.07(2), and a lease clause waiving them is void.

If a residential unit becomes untenantable, or has a substantial violation that materially affects health or safety, the tenant may move out unless the landlord promptly repairs. A tenant who stays gets rent reduced by the amount of lost use, but cannot withhold all rent.

Entry is governed by ATCP 134.09(2): only to inspect, make repairs, or show the unit to prospective tenants or purchasers. The landlord gives at least 12 hours of advance notice and enters at reasonable times, unless the tenant agrees to shorter notice or is away and the landlord reasonably believes entry is needed to protect the premises. The landlord announces before entering. A seller planning showings should schedule around that notice window.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Wisconsin houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Returning a security deposit

A residential landlord must deliver or mail the deposit, less lawful deductions, within 21 days after the tenancy ends. Wis. Stat. 704.28(4) counts the 21 days from the lease termination date if the tenant leaves then, from the start of a new tenant's term if the unit is re-rented early, or from the day the landlord learns the tenant has gone.

Standard deductions cover tenant damage, waste or neglect, unpaid rent, and certain unpaid utility charges. Other deductions require a separate written document titled "Nonstandard Rental Provisions," identified to the tenant before signing. ATCP 134.06 also bars a landlord from falsifying a claim against a deposit.

When the house sells, the deposit ledger should go with the lease. Ask the buyer to acknowledge the deposit amounts in writing.

Frequently asked questions

How many days notice must a Wisconsin landlord give to end a month-to-month tenancy?

At least 28 days in writing, ending at the end of a rental period, under Wis. Stat. 704.19. For unpaid rent, a month-to-month landlord can give a pay-or-vacate notice dated at least 5 days after it is given.

Does a tenant have to leave when the landlord sells?

No. A sale does not end a lease on its own. Under Wis. Stat. 704.09 the landlord's interest passes to the buyer, and covenants not personal to the original parties bind the successor.

How long does a landlord have to return a security deposit?

Within 21 days. Depending on the facts, s. 704.28(4) counts from the lease end, the start of a replacement tenancy, or the day the landlord learns the tenant moved out.

How much notice must a landlord give before entering a rental?

At least 12 hours, at reasonable times, unless the tenant agrees to less. ATCP 134.09(2) limits entry to inspections, repairs and showings to prospective tenants or purchasers, with limited exceptions.

Can a tenant withhold all rent for bad conditions?

No. Wis. Stat. 704.07(4) lets a tenant move out over untenantable conditions or cut rent in proportion to lost use. It does not allow full withholding while the tenant stays.

title: Wisconsin Eviction Notice Rules: Notice Types, Days and Selling the House
content:
Wisconsin Eviction Notice Rules: Notice Types, Days and Selling the House

Cash Home Buyers in Wisconsin
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Wisconsin Eviction Notice Rules: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Wisconsin Eviction Notice Rules sale
  • Turn the Wisconsin Eviction Notice Rules offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Wisconsin House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Wisconsin?
We buy Wisconsin houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Notice lengths by situation

The required notice turns on the kind of tenancy and the reason for ending it. Wis. Stat. 704.17 sets the baseline for missed rent: at least 5 days when the tenancy is month-to-month, week-to-week, or a lease of one year or less, and at least 30 days when the lease runs past a year.

SituationMinimum notice
Unpaid rent, month-to-month or week-to-weekPay or vacate at least 5 days out. A month-to-month tenant in default can instead get a vacate notice at least 14 days out.
Unpaid rent, lease of one year or less, or year-to-yearPay or vacate at least 5 days out. A second default within one year allows a 14-day vacate notice.
Other breach or waste, month-to-monthRemedy or vacate at least 5 days out, or a 14-day vacate notice
Other breach or waste, lease of one year or lessRemedy or vacate at least 5 days out. A repeat within one year allows a 14-day vacate notice.
Any default, lease longer than one yearAt least 30 days to pay, repair or comply
Criminal or drug-related activityVacate at least 5 days out, with no chance to remedy
No-fault end of a month-to-month tenancyAt least 28 days, ending at the close of a rental period

Rent, for this purpose, includes past due rent plus late fees owed on it, so one pay-or-vacate notice can demand both.

How a tenant cures a default

For a breach that is not about rent, the tenant is treated as complying by taking reasonable steps to fix the problem right after receiving the notice and sticking with the repair diligently. Another way to comply: where money damages would protect the landlord, the tenant makes a reasonable offer to pay them in good faith. Both tests appear in 704.17(1p)(b), (2)(b) and (3)(a).

Rent on a lease longer than a year is stricter. Everything owed must be paid by the date in the notice. If the tenant repeats a breach within a year of an earlier notice, the cure period disappears and the landlord may serve a 14-day vacate notice.

  • Criminal activity that threatens other tenants, neighbors or the landlord, and drug-related criminal activity on or near the premises, can end a tenancy on 5 days' notice with no cure period.
  • That notice has to describe the activity, give the date, name those involved, and explain the tenant's right to contest it in court.
  • A tenant who is the victim of the criminal activity is carved out under 704.17(3m)(c).
  • Under Wis. Stat. 704.16(3), a landlord can end the tenancy of someone whose acts put another tenant in the same building at imminent risk of serious physical harm, on at least 5 days' written notice, once one of the listed court filings or orders exists.

Delivering the notice

Put it in writing and deliver it by one of the methods in Wis. Stat. 704.21. After the termination date in a properly given notice, the tenant has no right to remain.

  • Hand it to the tenant, or leave it at the tenant's usual home with a family member at least 14 years old who is told what it says.
  • Leave a copy with a competent person in charge of the premises and mail a copy to the tenant's last-known address.
  • If those fail despite reasonable diligence, post it in a conspicuous place on the premises and mail a copy.
  • Send it by registered or certified mail to the tenant's last-known address.
  • Serve it the way a summons is served under Wis. Stat. 801.11.

A notice that skips the listed methods can still count if the tenant actually got it, but whoever claims receipt must prove it by clear and convincing evidence. Certified mail has a court perk: under Wis. Stat. 799.40(1g), the post office's proof of mailing is enough to show proper notice when the landlord files. For 28-day notices, 704.19(7) counts the day of giving as day one, and mail within Wisconsin is treated as given on the second day after mailing.

Can a lease or a mistake change the rules?

A lease cannot cut these protections down, except on leases longer than one year. Under 704.17(5), lease terms on ending a tenancy that conflict with the section are void apart from that one exception. A lease term that runs against the criminal activity rule in subsection (3m) is void on every lease.

Small errors do not always sink a notice. A rent notice with the wrong amount stays valid unless the landlord's figure was intentionally wrong or the tenant paid or tendered what the tenant believes is due (704.17(4m)). For a notice ending a periodic tenancy, an error that does not mislead does not void it, and a wrong termination date makes the notice effective on the first proper date after the one stated (704.19(4), (5)).

When the notice period ends

The landlord still has to go to court. A proper notice ends the tenant's right to occupy, but removal happens through an eviction action, handled in Wisconsin as a small claims case under chapter 799. Wis. Stat. 799.40(1) lets the person entitled to possession, or an agent authorized in writing, start it.

Taking back past due rent after the notice or after filing does not force a dismissal (799.40(1m)). In an eviction, the summons return date lands 5 to 25 days after issue, and the tenant must be served at least 5 days before that date (799.05(3)(b)). If the landlord wins, the court orders a writ of restitution and the sheriff carries it out under Wis. Stat. 799.44(2) and 799.45.

How a tenant affects selling a rented house

A tenant not in default keeps exclusive possession until the lease ends or a periodic tenancy is terminated. Wis. Stat. 704.05(2) lets the landlord show the premises to prospective purchasers on advance notice and at reasonable times, unless both sides signed a lease provision saying otherwise.

An owner who wants the house empty at closing should match the notice to the tenancy before picking a closing date. A no-fault month-to-month notice needs 28 days and must end at the close of a rental period. A default on a lease longer than a year needs 30 days. Selling with the tenant in place skips the notice and court steps altogether, and that can be weighed against how long removal would take.

A practical order of work: confirm the tenancy type from the lease, write and serve the right notice, keep proof of delivery, and only then set a closing date you can realistically meet. A cash buyer who accepts the house occupied removes most of that timeline risk.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Wisconsin houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

How many days is a Wisconsin eviction notice for unpaid rent?

Five days for a month-to-month, week-to-week, or one-year-or-shorter tenancy, and 30 days for a lease longer than one year. A month-to-month tenant in default can alternatively receive a 14-day vacate notice. The notice must be in writing and delivered by a method in Wis. Stat. 704.21.

Can a Wisconsin landlord evict without giving a chance to fix the problem?

In some cases, yes. A tenant who repeats a breach within one year can get a 14-day vacate notice. Criminal activity that threatens health or safety, and drug-related criminal activity on or near the premises, allow a 5-day notice with no cure period. A tenant who is the victim of the activity is excluded.

How long is the notice to end a month-to-month tenancy with no fault?

At least 28 days, in writing, ending at the close of a rental period. If rent is payable more often than monthly, a notice equal to the rent-paying period is enough. The notice must say the landlord intends to end the tenancy and give the date.

Does a Wisconsin landlord have to mail the eviction notice?

No. Wis. Stat. 704.21 lists several methods: handing it to the tenant, leaving it with a family member or person in charge plus mailing, posting plus mailing, certified mail, or service like a summons. Certified mail helps in court because proof of mailing is enough to show notice.

Is a notice enough to remove a tenant in Wisconsin?

No. Once the notice period runs out, the landlord must file an eviction action in court. If the landlord wins, the court orders a writ of restitution and the sheriff removes the tenant. The sheriff must carry out the writ within 10 days of receiving it.
